Le Cam’s Method

Classical Information Theory Foundations

1 Le Cam’s Method

We first upper bound the ability to distinguish two classical distributions p and q, as shown in the following lemma.

ImportantLemma

If two distributions p,q on set S = \{1,\cdots,n\} has total variance distance (TVD) \|p - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i = 1}^n|p(i) - q(i)| \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single sample algorithm \mathcal{A}: S \to \{p,q\} that \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing, in other words, satisfied \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2 and \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. It is sufficient to show that for an arbitrary algorithm \mathcal{A}, either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2. Notice that \begin{align} \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] + \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] & = 1 - \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] +\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p]\\ &\geq 1 - \sup_{U \subseteq S} \left |\text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[U] -\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[U]\right |\\ &= 1 - \|p - q\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \geq 1 - \varepsilon. \end{align} Then either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2, which means that either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \leq (1+\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \leq (1+\varepsilon)/2. ◻

A slight generalization of Lemma is to distinguish a unique distribution p_0 and multiple distributions p_1,\cdots,p_l for L =\{1,\cdots,l\}, where p_i are all distributions over set S=\{1,\cdots,n\}. We prove a generalized no-go theorem below:

ImportantLemma

If there exists a distribution \mathcal{D} over L such that \delta_{\mathcal{D}}:=\|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single-sampling algorithm that distinguishes p_0 between p_1,\cdots,p_l such that it is \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. We first directly prove this result using lemma. If it exists, we can use it as an algorithm that distinguishes the distribution q(i):=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}(i)] with p_0(i) and it is \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. This contradicts the fact that \|p_0 - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}} =\|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon according to Lemma. ◻

In Lemma, we can try all kinds of distribution \mathcal{D} over L and choose the hardest one \delta_{\mathrm{w}} = \min_{\mathcal{D}}\delta_{\mathcal{D}}. This reflects the worst case information complexity of this discrimination problem.

1.1 Problem Ensemble and Average Case Hardness

In general, this problem is much harder than two-point discrimination, as we are designing a unified algorithm that dealt with multiple two-point discrimination (p_0,p_1),\cdots,(p_0,p_L) at the same time. One can relax this problem by ensuring that the distribution p_i only appears following a fixed distribution \mathcal{D}. This reduces the problem to a two-point discrimination (p_0,\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}}p_r). Then the value \delta_{\mathcal{D}} in Lemma is tight. We call it the average case information complexity under problem ensemble \mathcal{D}. Similarly, we can define multiple-to-multiple tasks that discriminate a set of distribution \mathcal{A} from the other set of distribution \mathcal{B}, whose average case hardness is defined by \|\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}(A)}p_{r} -\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}(B)} q_{s}\|_{\mathrm{TVD}} for problem ensemble \mathcal{D}(\mathcal A) and \mathcal{D}(\mathcal B).

1.2 Replica Distinguishes Ensemble from Average

One confusing point is the discrimination of the distribution p_0 = \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}] and a set of distribution \{p_{r}\} with problem ensemble {r \sim \mathcal{D}}. By Lemma, we cannot distinguish them with probability greater than 1/2 given one-sample. However, under k-samples, this is equivalent to the discrimination of p_0(t_1)\cdots p_0(t_k) and a set of distribution \{p_{r}(t_1)\cdots p_{r}(t_k)\} with problem ensemble {r \sim \mathcal{D}}. We can check that \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}} \left[p_{r}(t_1)\cdots p_{r}(t_k)\right] \neq p_0(t_1)\cdots p_0(t_k) \\ = \left[\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}p_{r}(t_1)\right]\cdots \left[\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}p_{r}(t_k)\right], thus can be estimated with probability greater than 1/2.

1.3 Coarse Graining

Intuitively, distinguishing two fine-grained distributions is never more difficult than distinguishing their coarse-grained versions. With TVD, we quantify this intuition as Lemma.

ImportantLemma

Given two distribution \mathbf{p}:=\{p_1,\cdots,p_M\},\mathbf{q}:=\{q_1,\cdots,q_M\} and their coarse graining \mathbf{P}:=\bigcup_{s}\{p_{1,s},\cdots,p_{M,s}\},\mathbf{Q}:=\bigcup_{s}\{q_{1,s},\cdots,q_{M,s}\} such that \sum_{s} p_{k,s} = p_k,\sum_{s} q_{k,s} = q_k, \forall k \in \{1,\cdots,M\}. Then \|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \geq \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Since \|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} = 2^{-1}\|\cdot\|_{1}, we conclude that \|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}\|_{1} = \sum_{k,s}\|p_{k,s} - q_{k,s}\|_{1} \geq \sum_{k}\|\sum_{s}p_{k,s} - \sum_{s}q_{k,s}\|_{1} = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_{1} ◻

1.4 Le Cam’s Theorem

The most general form of the lemma is Le Cam’s bound. We prove this theorem and show that lemma is a special case of the Le-Cam theorem for completeness.

ImportantTheorem

Given a measurable space x \in \mathcal{X} and a family of measures P \in \mathcal{P}, P: 2^\mathcal{X} \to [0,1]. Let \hat \theta:\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^p be an arbitrary estimator of the parameters of this family of distributions \theta: \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}^p. Let D[\cdot,\cdot]:\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a pseudo-metric of the parameter space that is symmetric and satisfies the triangular inequality D(x,y)+D(y,z) \geq D(x,z). Take two arbitrary subsets \mathcal{P}_1, \mathcal{P}_2 \subset \mathcal{P} that satisfied \inf_{\substack{P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,P_2 \in \mathcal{P_2}} } D\left[\theta(P_1), \theta(P_2)\right] \geq 2\delta, then the inequality is true: \begin{align} \sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat \theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\ &\geq \delta\cdot \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \left[1 - \frac{1}{2}\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} [dP_1(x) - dP_2(x)]\right]. \end{align}

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. We first noted that \begin{align} 2\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\ &\geq \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP_1(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_1)\right] \\ &\quad + \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP_2(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_2)\right]. \end{align} Based on the triangular inequality, we have D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_1)\right] + D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_2)\right] \geq D\left[\theta(P_1),\theta(P_2)\right]\geq 2\delta. Thus, for a fixed point x, the tuple (f_1/2\delta,f_2/2\delta), \text{where }\begin{cases}f_1(x) =D[ \hat \theta(x),\theta(P_1)], \\f_2(x) =D[ \hat \theta(x),\theta(P_2)],\end{cases} is in the convex set \mathcal{S} =\{(r_1,r_2)\in \mathbb{R}^2| r_1,r_2\geq 0,r_1+r_2 \geq 1\}. Then \forall P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,\forall P_2 \in \mathcal{P}_2, we write the inequality \begin{align} 2\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\ &\geq 2\delta\cdot \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{[r_1(x),r_2(x)] \in \mathcal{S}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) + dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]\\ &\geq \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } 2\delta\cdot \\ &\quad \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{[r_1(x),r_2(x)] \in \mathcal{S}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) + dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]. \end{align} The RHS satisfied the identity \begin{align} \text{RHS} &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{ \substack{r_1(x),r_2(x)\geq 0,\\r_1(x)+r_2(x) = 1}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) +dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]\\ &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[1 +\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{ r_1(x)\in [0, 1]}\left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) - dP_2(x)\cdot r_1(x)\right]\right]\\ &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[1- \int_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X}\\P_2(x) \geq P_1(x)}} dP_2(x) - dP_1(x) \right]\\ &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[1- \frac{1}{2} \int_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X}}} |dP_2(x) - dP_1(x)| \right]. \end{align} This completes the proof. ◻

ImportantLemma

The lemma is a special case of the Le-Cam theorem.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Take the special case that \mathcal{X} = \{1,\cdots,n\}, \mathcal{P}_0 =\{p_0(x)\}, \mathcal{P}_1 =\{p_1(x),\cdots,p_l(x)\} and \theta(p_i) :=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }i =0,\\1&\text{else}.\end{cases} The estimator and metric are taken as \hat \theta(\cdot): \mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} and \begin{align} D(\cdot,\cdot): \{0,1\}^{2} \to \{0,1\}, \\ (\theta_1,\theta_2) &\hookrightarrow \begin{cases}1&\text{if }(\theta_1,\theta_2)=(1,0),(0,1),\\ 0 &\text{else}.\end{cases} \end{align} It is easy to see that D(\cdot,\cdot) is indeed symmetric and satisfies the triangular inequality. This strategy distinguished the \mathcal{P}_0 and \mathcal{P}_1 with success probability \begin{align} p_{\text{succ}} &=\min_{i=1,\cdots,l}\left\{ \text{Pr}_{x \sim p_0}[\hat \theta(x) =0 ],\text{Pr}_{x \sim p_i}[\hat \theta(x) =1 ]\right\} \\ &= 1 - \max_{i = 1,\cdots,l}\left\{ \text{Pr}_{x \sim p_0}[\hat \theta(x) =1 ],\text{Pr}_{x \sim p_i}[\hat \theta(x) =0 ]\right\}\\ &=1 - \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} E_{x \sim p} D[\hat \theta(x),\theta(p)]. \end{align} Based on Lemma, we conclude the inequality \begin{align} \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} E_{x \sim p} D[\hat \theta(x),\theta(p)] \geq \delta\cdot [1 - \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} ]. \end{align} Notice that \inf_{\substack{P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,P_2 \in \mathcal{P_2}} } D\left[\theta(P_1), \theta(P_2)\right] \geq 1, we take \delta = 1/2, which combine to the final result \begin{align} p_{\text{succ}} \leq 1 -\frac{1 - \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} }{2} = \frac{1 + \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} }{2} . \end{align} Then if \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon, we conclude that p_{\text{succ}}\leq (1+\varepsilon)/2 and cannot \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. ◻
